scenes.heading: Event Streams
scenes.narration: An event stream is an ordered, append-only log of events that many consumers can read independently.

scenes.heading: What defines a stream
bullets: Events are appended in order, never edited.
Each consumer tracks its own read position.
scenes.narration: A stream is an immutable log where new events are appended in sequence. Configurable retention means consumers can replay past events rather than losing them. Partitions preserve order within each partition while enabling parallel reads, and every consumer tracks its own offset independently.

scenes.heading: Reading from a stream
scenes.narration: Producers continuously append events, which the broker orders within each partition. A consumer reads from its current offset, processing events in order. As it finishes each event it advances its offset, so it always knows exactly where to resume after a restart.

scenes.heading: Stream log vs message queue
scenes.narration: An event stream keeps events in a durable log so multiple consumers can read and replay them at their own pace. A traditional queue usually deletes a message once it is consumed, focusing on handing work to a single worker. The stream's replayability is what makes it powerful for analytics and multiple downstream systems.

scenes.text: Event streams are ordered, replayable logs where many consumers read independently by offset, unlike queues that consume messages once.
scenes.narration: Because streams retain and reorder nothing, you can add new consumers or reprocess history at any time without disturbing existing ones.
